questions.explanation: QoS ensures responsiveness but does not provide security. Isolation is not merely administrative convenience; it limits attack surface by preventing access control from being targeted by general-network malware. Isolation does not prevent WiFi interference (different frequency bands). VLAN tagging is a networking construct, not a security measure against command spoofing; encryption of commands is required. Network isolation complements firewalls but does not replace them. QoS is traffic prioritization, not cybersecurity; firewalls, IDS, and encrypted commands provide actual security controls. Isolated VLAN segregates access control traffic from general building LAN, reducing exposure to compromised endpoints. However, if the VLAN is breached (e.g., rogue device injected, network tap installed), encrypted command/response is critical to prevent an attacker from sending unencrypted 'unlock door' commands to readers or controllers. IP-based systems must use TLS/SSL encryption for all server-to-reader communication. Defense-in-depth requires network isolation (VLAN), firewall rules, and cryptographic protection of access control commands to mitigate IP-based system vulnerabilities.

questions.explanation: PoE does not replace UPS backup; a UPS still backs the PoE switch to ensure 4–8 hours of offline operation during mains failure. PoE reduces cable types (power + data consolidated) but does not reduce total runs by 50%. Conduit pathways are similar whether using separate power or PoE. PoE is an electrical power delivery standard; RF shielding is determined by reader frequency (125 kHz, 13.56 MHz, BLE), not by power delivery method. PoE infrastructure (IEEE 802.3af/at) combines power and data over a single Ethernet cable, eliminating the need for separate 24V DC power pairs in conduit. This simplifies future reader replacements and upgrades without re-running power cables. Category 5e cabling supports PoE infrastructure (15.4 W per 802.3af port, 30 W per 802.3at port), making upfront investment in Cat 5e future-proof. Specifying Category 5e with PoE-capable infrastructure during initial installation enables cost-effective future upgrades to IP-based PoE readers without major re-cabling efforts.

questions.explanation: Mobile credentials incur cloud/app infrastructure costs, offsetting low per-card printing costs. Overall cost advantage is operational, not per-unit production. Mobile credentials operate at 2.4 GHz (BLE) or 13.56 MHz (NFC), not 125 kHz. RF frequency does not determine immunity to interception; encryption does. BLE and NFC are separate protocols; readers detect and use one or the other based on their capabilities. Readers do not automatically switch protocols. Mobile credentials (BLE/NFC via smartphone app) can be instantly revoked in real-time through the central access control server if the phone is lost, stolen, or employment terminates. Printed temporary cards remain valid for their entire validity window, creating a security window if cards are lost. Tokens are dynamically managed without physical distribution. Mobile credentials enable dynamic access revocation without physical card collection, improving security in high-turnover environments and reducing post-termination access breaches.

questions.explanation: Wiegand-based local panels cannot track state across multiple readers without extensive inter-panel communication. Relay modules lack intelligence for credential-level anti-passback logic. OSDP's 200–500 ms polling interval creates a 0.4–1 second lag, allowing double-entry attempts to slip through before the system registers the first badge swipe at the exit. Motion sensors prevent tailgating (multiple people passing through one badge swipe) but do not prevent anti-passback (same person, same credential, multiple entries without exits). IP-based centralized systems with sub-second event reporting enable real-time anti-passback logic at the server. When a credential swipes at an entry reader, the server logs the event and blocks the same credential from being used at the same entry until an exit event is recorded. This requires centralized state management and low-latency communication. Anti-passback rules require real-time, centralized credential state management; legacy panel-based systems cannot enforce this due to polling delays and lack of inter-panel synchronization.

questions.explanation: Monitoring cannot prevent cloning; a cloned card presents the same card ID as the original and is indistinguishable at the reader level. Post-hoc detection via pattern analysis (e.g., impossible travel between two locations) is possible but not foolproof. Smart cards do cost 2–3x more but provide encryption. RFID monitoring (live field strength detection) cannot eliminate cloning—an attacker can still capture the unencrypted card number passively. Facial recognition cross-check adds cost and operational friction; it does not address the root cause (unencrypted credential broadcast). It is a compensating control, not a replacement for secure credentials. Proximity card cloning occurs because unencrypted card numbers are broadcast openly. Monitoring/alerting on duplicate swipes can detect unauthorized access after the fact (forensic value) but cannot prevent a cloned card from being used to gain access. The cloning vulnerability persists at the protocol level. Smart cards with on-card encryption and mutual authentication eliminate cloning risk at the credential level. Proximity card cloning is a fundamental protocol vulnerability; monitoring mitigates risk post-access but does not prevent breach. Credential upgrade (smart card or biometric) is the only technical fix.

questions.explanation: Wiegand is half-duplex, not full-duplex. OSDP is also half-duplex (RS-485 serial) but supports bidirectional messages within the half-duplex constraint. Wiegand requires auxiliary modules, but OSDP is inherently bidirectional without external modules. Wiegand operates at 100 bits per second (fixed), while OSDP supports 9,600–115,200 bps variable data rates. Wiegand is a legacy, one-way protocol that transmits card data only; it cannot natively receive door lock status or REX signals from the controller. Auxiliary relay modules are needed for bidirectional feedback. OSDP (IEC 60839-11-5) is a bidirectional, secured protocol supporting real-time lock status, tamper alerts, power failure reporting, and biometric enrollments. Modern access control favors OSDP's bidirectional capability for real-time status monitoring, door health diagnostics, and secure credential transmission over legacy Wiegand's one-way design.

questions.explanation: Enrollment of 8–10 fingers reduces false rejection rate (FRR) but does not eliminate false acceptance. Biometric systems always have non-zero FAR due to template matching variance and spoofing risk (fake fingerprints). FAR of >5% would be unacceptable for high-security facilities. FRR of 2–5% is typical for fingerprint systems, causing legitimate users to be rejected occasionally. FAR is not exponentially sensitive to database size under proper algorithm implementation. NIST benchmarks control for database size, showing consistent FAR across 1,000–10,000 template databases. Fingerprint readers achieve FAR of 0.01–0.1% (1 false acceptance per 1,000–10,000 attempts) at industry-standard security levels. For high-security areas (cash handling, server rooms), this residual error rate requires secondary authentication such as manual visual verification by a security officer or a PIN code to ensure no unauthorized access occurs. High-security facilities should implement multi-factor authentication combining biometrics (fingerprint) with secondary factors (PIN, guard verification) to mitigate the residual FAR risk.
